title: The World After Rome
description: How Europe, Islam, and Asia reshaped themselves after Rome's fall

concepts.title: The Early Medieval West
concepts.contentHtml:
When the Western Roman Empire collapsed in 476 CE, it left a power vacuum that Germanic kingdoms rushed to fill. The Franks, Visigoths, Ostrogoths, and Anglo-Saxons carved up the old Roman world. Roads crumbled, long-distance trade contracted, literacy narrowed.

The Catholic Church became the great continuity — monasteries preserved Latin learning, bishops governed cities, and the Pope in Rome claimed spiritual authority over the fractured West.

In 800 CE, Charlemagne (King of the Franks) was crowned Emperor of the Romans by Pope Leo III — the first attempt to reunite Europe under one Christian ruler since Rome. His empire divided after his death in 814, but it set the template for medieval kingship.

concepts.title: The Rise of Islam
concepts.contentHtml:
In 622 CE, the Prophet Muhammad fled Mecca for Medina — the Hijra, the starting point of the Islamic calendar. Within a century of his death (632 CE), Arab armies had conquered the Arabian Peninsula, Persia, Egypt, North Africa, and Spain.

The speed was extraordinary: the Umayyad Caliphate (661–750 CE) stretched from Portugal to the Indus River, the largest empire the world had yet seen.

Islam unified diverse peoples through a shared faith, language (Arabic), and legal system (Sharia). The Abbasid Caliphate (750–1258 CE), centered on Baghdad, presided over one of history's great intellectual flowerings — the Islamic Golden Age.

concepts.title: Byzantium and the East
concepts.contentHtml:
The Byzantine Empire — the surviving Eastern Roman Empire — remained a major power throughout the early medieval period. Emperor Justinian I (r. 527–565 CE) briefly reconquered parts of the West, codified Roman law into the Corpus Juris Civilis, and built the Hagia Sophia in Constantinople.

Meanwhile, the Tang Dynasty (618–907 CE) in China was arguably the most sophisticated civilization on Earth — cosmopolitan, artistically brilliant, with a population of 80 million. The Silk Road continued to move goods, peoples, and ideas between East and West.

In India, the Gupta Empire had already produced what scholars call the Indian Golden Age — Hindu mathematics, astronomy, literature, and the concept of zero that would later travel to Europe via the Arabs.

title: Feudalism and the Crusades
description: Lords, knights, serfs, and the wars for the Holy Land

concepts.title: The Feudal System
concepts.contentHtml:
Feudalism was the political and economic system that organized medieval Europe from roughly the 9th to 14th centuries. It rested on a hierarchy of land and service.

The king granted land (fiefs) to nobles (lords) in exchange for military service. Lords sub-granted land to knights for the same reason. At the bottom, serfs — tied to the land and unable to leave — farmed the fields and owed labor to their lord.

This system emerged from chaos: Vikings raided from the north, Magyars from the east, Saracens from the south. Lords who could protect peasants gained followers. By the 10th century, feudal relationships structured most of European life — political power was essentially personal, local, and militarized.

concepts.title: The Crusades (1095–1291)
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1095, Pope Urban II called upon European knights to recapture Jerusalem — then under Seljuk Turkish control — promising spiritual rewards. Thousands responded in the First Crusade, which captured Jerusalem in 1099.

There were nine major Crusades over two centuries. The Third Crusade (1189–1192) pitted Richard I of England ('the Lionheart') against Saladin, the Kurdish Muslim sultan of Egypt and Syria. They fought to a stalemate; Saladin kept Jerusalem but allowed Christian pilgrims access.

The Crusades had complex effects: they intensified Christian–Muslim tensions, exposed Europe to Islamic science and trade goods, and helped shift wealth and power toward Italian merchant cities like Venice and Genoa.

concepts.title: Saladin and the Islamic World
concepts.contentHtml:
Saladin (Salah ad-Din, 1137–1193) united Egypt and Syria, recaptured Jerusalem in 1187, and became a symbol of chivalry even in Christian Europe — his magnanimity to defeated Crusaders was widely noted. His Ayyubid dynasty balanced military genius with Islamic scholarship and statecraft.

The Islamic world during the Crusades was not monolithic. The Abbasid Caliphate in Baghdad, the Fatimids in Egypt, and the Seljuk Turks all had competing interests. Saladin's genius was forging these into a coherent coalition.

Outside the Crusader theater, the Islamic world stretched from Spain to Central Asia — producing philosophers like Ibn Rushd (Averroes), who preserved and extended Aristotle, and Ibn Sina (Avicenna), whose medical canon was used in Europe for 500 years.

title: The Mongol Empire and the Black Death
description: The greatest land empire in history and the plague that reshaped Eurasia

concepts.title: Genghis Khan and the Mongol Conquests
concepts.contentHtml:
Temüjin, born around 1162, unified the feuding Mongol tribes and proclaimed himself Genghis Khan ('Universal Ruler') in 1206. He then launched the most rapid territorial expansion in history.

By his death in 1227, the Mongols had conquered Central Asia and much of northern China and Persia, and had raided into Eastern Europe. His successors pushed further: the Yuan Dynasty (grandson Kublai Khan) controlled China by 1271; the Ilkhanate controlled Persia.

The Mongol conquests were catastrophic in human cost — estimates range from 30 to 40 million dead, roughly 10% of the world's population. Baghdad fell in 1258; the Abbasid Caliph was executed, ending the golden age of Islamic scholarship.

concepts.title: The Pax Mongolica and its Legacy
concepts.contentHtml:
After conquest came consolidation. The Pax Mongolica ('Mongol Peace', c. 1250–1350) allowed unprecedented trade across Eurasia. The Silk Road revived under Mongol protection. Marco Polo traveled from Venice to China and back under this umbrella.

Mongol rulers proved often adaptable. Kublai Khan adopted Chinese administration. Ilkhan rulers in Persia converted to Islam. The Golden Horde that ruled the Russian steppe also became Muslim.

West African empires flourished independently during this period. The Mali Empire under Mansa Musa (r. 1312–1337) controlled the gold and salt trades across the Sahara. Mansa Musa's 1324 pilgrimage to Mecca — with 60,000 attendants and 12 tons of gold — was so extravagant it caused inflation across North Africa and the Middle East.

concepts.title: The Black Death (1347–1353)
concepts.contentHtml:
The Black Death — bubonic plague caused by Yersinia pestis — arrived in Sicily in 1347 via Genoese trading ships from the Black Sea. It swept across Europe over five years, killing an estimated 30–60% of Europe's population.

Cities were devastated. Florence lost perhaps 50–60% of its residents. The social consequences were enormous: the feudal system was disrupted as surviving peasants demanded higher wages; the Church lost prestige as prayer failed to stop the dying; and a mood of nihilism mixed with intense piety swept the arts.

The plague had already killed millions in China and the Middle East — it traveled along the very Silk Road the Mongols had reopened. A reminder that global connectivity accelerates the spread of everything, pathogens included.

title: The Islamic Golden Age
description: How medieval Islam preserved and transformed world knowledge

concepts.title: The House of Wisdom
concepts.contentHtml:
Under the Abbasid Caliph Harun al-Rashid and his son al-Ma'mun, Baghdad became the world's intellectual capital. The Bayt al-Hikma (House of Wisdom, founded c. 830 CE) was a translation bureau and research institution that translated Greek, Persian, and Indian texts into Arabic.

The scope was staggering: Aristotle, Euclid, Ptolemy, Galen, and Sanskrit mathematical texts all became accessible in Arabic. Scholars then built on these foundations rather than merely preserving them.

Al-Khwarizmi (c. 780–850) developed algebra — the word comes from his treatise title al-Kitab al-mukhtasar fi hisab al-jabr wal-muqabala. His name gives us the word 'algorithm'. He popularized the Hindu-Arabic numeral system that replaced Roman numerals across Europe.

concepts.title: Science, Medicine, and Philosophy
concepts.contentHtml:
Ibn Sina (Avicenna, 980–1037) wrote the Canon of Medicine — a medical encyclopedia used as the standard European textbook until the 17th century. He described contagious disease, quarantine, and clinical trials 700 years before they were accepted in Europe.

Ibn al-Haytham (Alhazen, 965–1040) founded modern optics. His Book of Optics explained vision, refraction, and the camera obscura based on experiment rather than speculation — an early scientific method.

In North Africa and Spain (al-Andalus), Ibn Rushd (Averroes, 1126–1198) wrote commentaries on Aristotle so influential that European scholars called him simply 'The Commentator'. His work helped trigger the European rediscovery of Aristotle and, ultimately, the Renaissance.

concepts.title: How Islamic Knowledge Reached Europe
concepts.contentHtml:
Islamic learning reached medieval Europe through three main routes:

Spain (al-Andalus) — Córdoba under Caliph Abd al-Rahman III (r. 912–961) was Europe's largest city, with libraries of 400,000 volumes. Christian scholars came to translate Arabic texts into Latin.

Sicily: under Arab rule from the 9th to the 11th century, later Norman, the island was a bilingual mixing ground where Arabic scholarship entered Italian intellectual life.

Crusader contacts — Despite the violence, Crusaders brought back scientific and mathematical knowledge from the Islamic world.

The Toledo School of Translators (12th century) was the most systematic effort: scholars like Gerard of Cremona translated over 80 Arabic works, giving Europe Euclid, Ptolemy, Avicenna, and Aristotle in Latin.

title: The Late Middle Ages and Medieval Legacy
description: Crisis, resilience, and the foundations of modernity

concepts.title: Crises of the 14th Century
concepts.contentHtml:
The 14th century was a century of crises. The Black Death, the Hundred Years' War (1337–1453) between England and France, the Great Famine (1315–1322), and the Western Schism (competing popes, 1378–1417) all undermined established institutions simultaneously.

Out of crisis came transformation. Joan of Arc (1412–1431), a peasant girl who claimed divine visions, led French armies to a series of victories and helped turn the tide of the Hundred Years' War before being captured by the English-allied Burgundians, handed to the English and burned at the stake at Rouen. She became a symbol of French national identity.

The peasant revolts — the Jacquerie in France (1358) and the English Peasants' Revolt (1381) — showed the feudal order was fracturing under the pressure of post-plague demographics and rising expectations.

concepts.title: New Powers: Ottoman Empire and Aztec Civilization
concepts.contentHtml:
As medieval Europe fragmented, new powers rose on its margins. The Ottoman Turks expanded from Anatolia into the Balkans, and in 1453 Sultan Mehmed II conquered Constantinople — ending the Byzantine Empire and closing the eastern land route to Asia. This would help spur European exploration westward.

On the other side of the world, the Aztec (Mexica) Empire built Tenochtitlán — a city of 200,000 on a lake, larger than any contemporary European capital — and dominated central Mexico from 1428. Their sophisticated society, calendar, agriculture, and architecture developed entirely independently of the Old World.

In southern Africa, Great Zimbabwe (12th–15th centuries) was the capital of a trading empire that exported gold to India and China, evidence that medieval Africa had complex, internationally connected civilizations.

concepts.title: What the Middle Ages Left Behind
concepts.contentHtml:
The Middle Ages is often caricatured as a dark, stagnant gap between Rome and the Renaissance — a misconception. Medieval contributions were profound:

— Universities: Bologna (1088), Oxford (c. 1096), Paris (c. 1150) — the medieval university model is still the world's template.
— Gothic architecture: Engineering feats that pushed stone to its limits, letting in light through stained glass.
— Common law: The English legal tradition — jury trials, habeas corpus, Magna Carta (1215) — shapes modern democracies.
— Agricultural revolution: Three-field rotation, the heavy plow, and the horse collar transformed medieval European food production.

And critically: the Islamic Golden Age transmitted the intellectual heritage of Greece, Persia, and India to Europe. The Renaissance and Scientific Revolution built on medieval shoulders.

title: Byzantine Empire
description: The Roman Empire that didn't fall in 476

concepts.title: Continuity from Rome
concepts.contentHtml:
The Eastern Roman (Byzantine) Empire continued for nearly 1000 years after the West fell. Capital: Constantinople. The Byzantines called themselves Romans (Rhomaioi); 'Byzantine' is a modern label.

Justinian I (527-565) tried to reconquer the West and codified Roman law in the Corpus Juris Civilis — the foundation of modern civil-law systems. Hagia Sophia (built 537) showcased Byzantine engineering.

concepts.title: Religion and Schism
concepts.contentHtml:
Byzantine Christianity differed from Western (Latin) Catholicism in liturgy, language (Greek vs Latin), papal authority, and theological details. The Great Schism of 1054 formally divided Christianity into Catholic (West) and Orthodox (East).

Byzantine missions converted the Slavs (Bulgaria, Russia, Serbia). Cyril and Methodius created the Glagolitic script for translating scripture; their disciples later developed Cyrillic, named in Cyril's honor. Russia inherited Byzantine Orthodox traditions; Moscow saw itself as the 'Third Rome' after Constantinople fell.

concepts.title: The Long Decline
concepts.contentHtml:
From the 11th century, Byzantium was pressed by Seljuk Turks, Crusaders (who shockingly sacked Constantinople in the Fourth Crusade, 1204), Italian merchants, and finally the Ottomans.

The 1453 Ottoman conquest of Constantinople ended the empire. Greek scholars fleeing west helped catalyze the Italian Renaissance.

Byzantine influences persist: Eastern Orthodox Christianity, Cyrillic script, civil-law codes, Hagia Sophia (a museum from 1934, a mosque again since 2020), mosaic and icon traditions.

concepts.title: Agricultural Revolution
concepts.contentHtml:
The medieval European agricultural revolution dramatically increased productivity. The heavy plow (capable of working dense northern soils), three-field crop rotation, horse collars (allowing horses to plow), and watermills/windmills transformed agriculture.

Population grew significantly — from ~30 million in Europe in 1000 CE to ~75 million by 1300. Cities grew with surplus food. Population was knocked back by the Black Death (1347-1351, ~30-50% mortality), but eventually rebounded.

concepts.title: Universities & Scholasticism
concepts.contentHtml:
Medieval universities — Bologna (~1088), Paris (~1150), Oxford (~1167), Cambridge (1209) — emerged as new institutions. They developed standardized curricula (trivium, quadrivium), credentials, and faculties.

Scholastic philosophers (Aquinas, Anselm, Abelard) attempted to integrate Christian theology with Aristotelian philosophy. The model has shaped Western academic thought ever since.

Translations of Aristotle and Islamic scholarship into Latin in the 12th-13th centuries fueled this intellectual revival. Medieval universities were the institutional ancestors of modern ones.

concepts.title: Technological Innovations
concepts.contentHtml:
Medieval Europe saw substantial technological advances:

• Printing: Gutenberg's movable-type press (~1450) revolutionized communication.
• Eyeglasses: ~1280 in Italy.
• Mechanical clocks: 13th century, transforming time-keeping.
• Gunpowder weapons: spreading from China by ~1300.
• Improved ships: caravels enabling Atlantic exploration by ~1450.

The 'Dark Ages' label is increasingly rejected by historians — medieval Europe was technologically and intellectually dynamic, especially after 1000.

concepts.title: The Black Death
concepts.contentHtml:
The Black Death (bubonic and pneumonic plague) reached Europe in 1347 via Genoese ships from Crimea. Within four years it killed ~30-50% of Europe's population — perhaps 25-50 million dead, in a continent of ~75 million.

Massive social, economic, and religious consequences. Labor shortages strengthened peasant bargaining power, accelerating the decline of serfdom. The Church's authority was shaken when prayers didn't prevent the catastrophe.

Plague returned in waves for centuries. London's Great Plague of 1665 was England's last major outbreak; Marseille's in 1720 was among the last in western Europe.

concepts.title: Late Medieval Crisis
concepts.contentHtml:
The 14th century was rough beyond the plague. The Hundred Years' War between England and France (1337-1453); the Western Schism (two and three popes claiming legitimacy); famines from climate cooling.

Yet the late Middle Ages also saw vernacular literature flourish (Chaucer, Dante, Boccaccio). Renaissance humanism began in Italy. Critique of Church corruption laid groundwork for Reformation.

concepts.title: Transition to Modernity
concepts.contentHtml:
The medieval-to-modern transition is gradual. Conventional dates: fall of Constantinople (1453), Gutenberg's Bible (~1455), Columbus reaching the Americas (1492), Luther's Theses (1517).

Each marks something: the end of Eastern Rome; mass communication; European globalism; religious schism. Together they reshaped Europe and the world.

The Middle Ages didn't end at a single moment — early modern periods overlap, regions transitioned at different paces. The shift from medieval to modern feudal/agricultural to capitalist/industrial took centuries.
